faq_slots.question: How long does it take to decorate a room?
faq_slots.answer_brief: The facts pack gives no standard duration for any decorating job, so give what decides it and no number unless [CV: typical_jobs] confirms one: the state of the surfaces and the preparation they need before paint (filling, stripping, sealing), how much woodwork there is, and the drying between coats, which follows the paint's own instructions and the warmth and air in the room rather than the clock. faq_slots.question: Why does paint keep peeling off my walls or woodwork?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Use the assigned symptom's meaning and its linked local issue. Three genuinely different causes in plain words, from the trade facts done badly rows: moisture behind the paint (a damp wall or wet timber painted over, so the film lifts); a surface the paint could never hold to (dust, loose old paint, grease or a shiny finish under it, with no key or primer); a stain or an old loose layer that was never sealed or taken off, so each new coat comes away with it. Then what the local housing adds (older layers of paint, pebbledash and render, fresh plaster on a new estate), then the fix: the cause dealt with, the loose paint off, the bare areas primed, before any finish. Never that another coat will hold it.

faq_slots.question: Is it better to paint over wallpaper or strip it?
faq_slots.answer_brief: From the trade facts painting over wallpaper row: sound, well stuck paper can be painted after the seams are checked and the right preparation is used, and some papers bubble or lift under a water based primer, so it is not always the better answer; paper that is lifting, bubbled or layered is stripped. What decides it is the state of the paper and the wall under it, never a general rule. No product named.

faq_slots.question: How long does new plaster need before it can be painted?
faq_slots.answer_brief: From the trade facts plaster drying and new plaster first coat rows: plaster has to be properly dry before ordinary paint goes on, and how long that takes depends on the wall, the plaster and how warm and aired the room is, so give no number of days or weeks; it shows as the colour evening out and the darker patches going. On bare plaster the paint goes on thinned for its first coat where the paint's instructions call for it, so it goes into the surface rather than sitting on it; painting too soon traps the water and the paint flakes or blisters. No product named.

faq_slots.question: Do I need permission to repaint the outside of my house?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Point at the trade facts rule rows (Table C) and write what usually applies, with "usually" or "in most cases": repainting a house in its existing colour usually needs no application; a listed home can need consent where the change touches what makes it special (a new colour, painting brick or stone that was never painted, taking off old plaster inside), and in some conservation areas a local restriction can take away the right to change the colour of the front. What the customer does about it only as the row gives it (check with the council before the work; whether the business handles that only from [CV: handles_planning]). Never an Act's, an order's or a direction's name, no figure.

cards.title: A room that's ready for a new colour
cards.brief: A situation card, not a fault: the household wants a change (a colour on the walls, paper in the hall, the woodwork back to white, a kitchen that feels new without new units). What decides it: what is on the surfaces now (filled holes, old gloss, a wall papered twice, a textured ceiling, fresh plaster), because that sets the preparation and how the finish reads when the light comes across it. What the work gives them, in plain words from the trade facts stages: the surface cleaned, made good, sanded and sealed where it is bare or stained, then the finish coats, then the colour. On a Painter page the card reads as the interior refresh, the wallpaper or the units; on a Painter and Decorator page as the plain wall the owner wants to carry a painted effect or a mural, and the sound, primed base it needs first. Light and surfaces, never trends; never a lifestyle pitch, never a fault invented for it.
cards.mechanism: what is on the surface now, which sets the preparation

cards.title: Paint lifting off sills, frames and doors
cards.brief: Problem led: paint flaking from sills, window frames, doors and fascias, bare wood showing through, a sill that gives under a thumb, putty falling out (the trade facts signs rows for exterior painting, woodwork and sash windows). The one cause this card makes: the paint film opened by the weather on the sunny, rain facing sides of the house, so water gets under it and the timber starts to take it in. Say what the fix usually involves from the stages: the loose paint off back to a firm edge, soft wood repaired, bare areas primed, undercoat and finish, in dry weather, because damp timber holds moisture under new paint. Exterior copy spends its words on the timber, not the walls. On older paintwork the layers are assessed before they are stripped, as the normal first step, never a claim about the reader's house. Never that another coat will cure it; not the walls (card 3 owns them).
cards.mechanism: the paint film opened by the weather, letting water under it

cards.title: Walls where paint blisters, flakes or stains come back
cards.brief: Problem led: inside, a mark on a ceiling back within weeks of being painted over, paint coming off in sheets, a patch that reads darker or duller than the rest; outside, masonry paint blistering, green growth back within a season, white salts showing through (the trade facts signs and done badly rows). The one cause this card makes: paint put onto a surface it could not hold to, or that was still carrying moisture or a stain (dust, loose old paint, an unsealed repair, a damp wall). More paint over the same fault fails the same way, in the brief's own words. Say what the fix usually involves from the stages: the cause of any damp found and dealt with first, the loose material off, the stain sealed with a primer that stops it, repairs sealed so they do not drink the paint, then the finish; an old solid wall given a finish that lets it breathe where the facts row has it. Never a promise the stain or the growth will not return where the cause is still live. Not timber (card 2 owns it).
cards.mechanism: paint put onto dust, loose paint, damp or a stain it could not hold to

cards.title: Units, doors and stairs you want kept, not replaced
cards.brief: A situation card: the kitchen carcasses are sound and the room works as it is, the doors, the staircase or a wardrobe just look tired, chipped at the handles or gone yellow. What decides it: the finish that is on them now (old gloss, lacquer, grease by the handles, worn varnish), which a new coat will not hold to unless it is cleaned, rubbed back to a key and primed with a primer that grips, from the trade facts furniture and woodwork stages (degrease, take off the loose finish and dull the shiny one, repair, primer, finish coats, left to dry before the doors go back on). What the work gives them: the piece kept and the finish renewed, by brush or sprayed; spray and brush are two methods, not a ranking (the trade facts). On a Painter and Decorator page the same, or a painted effect on a piece. White gloss gone yellow is the old solvent based finish ageing, most away from daylight (the trade facts), never a fault in the house. No claim about how long a painted kitchen lasts.
cards.mechanism: a shiny or greasy finish that new paint will not grip without a key

cards.title: The first signs
cards.brief: The things a homeowner notices first, from the trade facts signs row for this service, in their words: the gloss peeling, hairline cracks, putty falling out, a sash that sticks, a crack that has come back, a chip in a coating on steel. The one cause this card makes: the job left undone. Then what it leads to if left, from the skipped row: specific, never alarming. On a schedule led page (exterior repainting on a cycle, commercial decorating between tenancies, fire protection coatings) the card is what slips and when: the film on the sunny sides dulls, then cracks, then lets water in and the timber greys; corridor walls scuffed through to the plaster before the next cycle; a coating chipped back to bare steel, so it is no longer what was tested; with the reason in the sun, the rain, the traffic or the steel, never in the customer's diary.

cards.title: Damp or a stain that keeps coming back
cards.brief: Paint that has been redone and failed the same way: the mark back on the ceiling, blisters again on the same wall, mould back in the same corner, paint lifting again on the same stretch of render. The one cause this card makes: a source of water that is still live (a leak above, condensation, water getting in through cracked render or open joints) feeding the surface, so every new coat is painted onto a problem that has not stopped. Say what the job does first from the trade facts stages: the cause found and dealt with before any paint, the surface left to dry, loose material off, then sealed and finished; never a promise the mark or the mould stays away while the cause is live. Never a dig at the last decorator. On an Artex page: a damaged or dropping textured ceiling, with testing before anything is touched (the trade facts), never removal instructions.
cards.mechanism: a source of water that is still live, feeding the surface

cards.title: Bare wood, soft spots and open joints
cards.brief: Grey bare wood on a sill, a soft spot under a thumb, putty gone from the glass, a joint open at the corner of a frame, a fascia with no paint left on it (the trade facts signs rows). The one cause this card makes: timber taking in water once there is nothing left on it to keep the water out, so it swells, the joints open and the wood starts to decay. Say what the job does from the stages: decayed wood cut out and new pieced in rather than the whole window replaced, joints and putty made good, bare timber primed before any finish, the sashes painted so the paint never reaches the cords and the moving parts, and new putty left to reach the state its maker says can be painted. Older paintwork assessed before it is stripped and never burned off with a flame, as the normal method. On an interior page the card reads as the woodwork: white gloss gone yellow (the old solvent based finish ageing, most away from daylight), doors and skirting chipped through, varnish worn to the wood. Not the film opened by the weather: the category page owns that.
cards.mechanism: timber taking in water once nothing is left on it

cards.title: Past the point of touching up

On a schedule led page: the point on a cycle where a wash down and a recoat no longer holds because what is under the finish is soft or loose, from the done badly row. Not a live source of water: card 2 owns that.
cards.mechanism: a background that has broken down under the finish

cards.brief: The customer's situation: they want the room, the hall, the kitchen or a piece of furniture to look different, and the bones are fine (the plaster sound, the carcasses solid, the layout as they want it). What decides it: the surface as it is now (fresh plaster, old paper, a shiny finish, a textured ceiling, a wall with a history of filler), which sets what has to happen first and whether the result will hold. What the work gives them, from the trade facts stages for this service: on an interior painting page the colour on walls and woodwork; on a wallpapering page a papered wall or a whole hall, lined first where the wall is uneven; on a furniture and kitchen page the units kept and the doors repainted; on a spray painting page units and doors given a smooth sprayed finish where the room can be masked and aired; on a coving page a clean line where wall meets ceiling; on a decorative finishes page a plain wall carrying a painted effect or a mural on a sound, primed base. Never a fault invented for it, never a lifestyle pitch: the surface and the room, not the dream.
cards.mechanism: the surface as it is now, which sets what has to happen first

cards.title: How it will look when the light comes across it
cards.brief: The customer's situation: they have seen patchy walls, seams that show, brush marks on doors and bubbles in paper in other houses, and want to know what stops that happening in theirs. What decides it: the preparation and the method, which they will never see once it is done: holes filled and rubbed flat, a repair sealed so it does not drink the paint, lining paper on a wall that is not flat, a key and a primer on a shiny door, a plumb line and a pattern match, the masking and the clean air that spraying needs, the adhesive set before a cove is decorated (the trade facts stages and done badly rows for this service). What the work gives them: a finish that holds up in daylight across the wall. One specific from the stages for this service; never a dig at another trade.
cards.mechanism: the preparation under the finish, which shows in low light

cards.title: Which way of doing it suits the room
cards.brief: The customer's situation: they are weighing two or three ways of doing it (paint against paper, a plain matt against a washable finish, water based against solvent based on the woodwork, hand painted against sprayed units, lining paper against a skim, one cove profile against another, a painted effect against a patterned paper). What decides it: the surface, how the room is used (a hall that gets knocked, a bathroom's steam, a kitchen's grease), the light and how it will be cleaned, from the trade facts materials and methods cell for this service. What the work gives them: the option that suits that room, never the one that is best in general; spray and brush are two methods, not a ranking (the trade facts). A named product only from [CV: materials_methods]. No claim about how long a finish lasts or what it costs unless the rows or the client values give it.
cards.mechanism: the room's use and light deciding the method

cards.title: What it will need from you afterwards
cards.brief: The customer's situation: they want to know what they are taking on once the job is done: when the room can be used, when the doors go back on the units, how long before a paintable paper can be painted, how the finish is cleaned, when a touch up will show. What decides it: the drying and the hardening, which follow the paint's own instructions and the warmth and air in the room rather than the clock (the trade facts: the adhesive dry before paper is painted, the doors back on only once the finish has dried, the cove adhesive set before it is decorated), and what the finish was chosen for. What the work gives them: an honest picture of what the new surface will put up with and what it will not. Aftercare advice as this business's own only when aftercare_advice is confirmed. No times, no promise about how it will look or last.
cards.mechanism: drying that follows the paint and the room, not the clock

cards.title: Older houses with paint laid on paint
cards.brief: The town's housing era from the profile (Victorian and Edwardian terraces with timber sash windows and lime plaster, interwar semis with pebbledash or render, post war homes with textured ceilings). The one cause this card makes: layers of paint and coatings built up over the decades on the town's older timber, walls and ceilings. Tie the era to what it means for the work, never to a judgement on anyone's paintwork: old paint layers assessed before they are sanded or stripped, and never burned off with a flame; a textured ceiling tested, or treated as if it holds asbestos, before it is disturbed; an old solid wall given a finish that lets it breathe (the trade facts rows), said as the normal first step. Older homes can have lead in earlier layers and asbestos in older textured coatings: never that a street or a house does, never removal instructions. Not what is under one surface: the service pages own that.
cards.mechanism: layers of paint and coatings built up over the decades

cards.title: Outside walls and timber facing the weather
cards.brief: The town's exposure from the profile: coastal salt air, a hilltop that catches wind driven rain, fronts that face south or west, a valley that stays damp. The one cause this card makes: the weather the town's elevations face, which decides which sills, frames, doors and rendered fronts fail first and how long they stay wet. What it means for the work in plain words: the weather side needs more preparation and waits for a dry, settled spell, because damp timber and masonry hold moisture under new paint (the trade facts exterior rows); pebbledash and render that hold water blister paint sooner where their cracks are left. Never that the town's houses are peeling or overdue; never a temperature. Not the paint film opened by the weather as such: the category page owns that.
cards.mechanism: the weather the town's elevations face

cards.title: New builds and fresh plaster
cards.brief: The profile's new estates, extensions and loft conversions. The one cause this card makes: plaster still drying out in a new or newly extended home. What it means for the work: fresh plaster has to be properly dry before ordinary paint goes on, the first coat is a thinned one where the paint's instructions call for it, and the hairline cracks that open as a new house dries are filled after that coat, when they can be seen (the trade facts plaster rows); painting too soon traps the water and the paint flakes or blisters. No number of days or weeks, no promise about a developer's finish, never a judgement on the estate.
cards.mechanism: plaster still drying out in a new or newly extended home

cards.title: Shops, offices and lets turned round between tenants
cards.brief: The town's commercial mix from the profile: a high street, offices, lets and HMOs, a school or a surgery. The one cause this card makes: a building that has to stay in use while it is decorated, so the work is phased round the people, the trades and the opening hours in it (the trade facts commercial row). What it means for the work: access and sequence agreed before the first day, finishes chosen for how the walls will be cleaned, a landlord's rooms redecorated between tenancies; out of hours work as an arrangement for a job, never a given, and only from the client values. Written only where the services list has a Commercial decorating page; otherwise the card reads as the town's rented homes between tenants. Never fixed hours, never a fire rating or a class promised.
cards.mechanism: a building that has to stay in use while it is decorated

cost.h2: What Affects the Cost of [WORK] in [TOWN]

cards.title: Tall stairwells, bay fronts and getting up to it
cards.brief: Where the town's houses are tall terraces with long stairwells, or fronts with bays and no room for a tower, the work needs more access and more time; parking for the van and somewhere for a scaffold matter on a tight street. Say why that adds time; the town profile says which streets are which. No figure, never a scaffold promised.

cards.title: The age of the surfaces
cards.brief: Older paint layers, lime plaster, textured ceilings and sash windows take assessment, testing or slower methods before they can be touched, and more making good after. From the profile's housing era only, said as what the work meets and never as a judgement on the houses. No figure.

cards.title: Conservation areas and listed homes
cards.brief: Where the town has conservation areas or listed buildings, a change of colour outside or a window repair can need checking with the council first, which adds time before the work can start. "Usually", never the order's, the area's or the Act's name. From the dossier rules only; whether the business handles it only from [CV: handles_planning].

cards.title: The weather side of the house
cards.brief: An exposed front or a seafront elevation needs more preparation and a settled spell to paint, so an outside job there takes longer than the same wall in a sheltered street. From the profile where it gives the exposure. A day moved by the weather and rebooked only from weather_delays_rebooked. No figure.

faq_slots.answer_brief: Prices only from [CV: price_list]; otherwise the things that push the price up in a town like this (the age of the surfaces, tall or awkward access, an exposed front) and how the quote is given, from [CV: quote_method] only.

faq_slots.answer_brief: From [CV: start_time] and [CV: response_time] only. The town is in the area covered; nothing about distance unless [CV: travel_distance] is set.

faq_slots.question: Do you cover [TOWN]?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Yes: the town and the villages around it (code lists them; name none). How the business reaches it from its base only from the client values. Link one page in this town.

faq_slots.question: Do you guarantee your work in [TOWN]?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Start with yes, then the terms from [CV: guarantee_years] and [CV: guarantee_scope]. Described, never promised.

faq_slots.question: Are you insured?
faq_slots.answer_brief: The cover figure from [CV: insurance_cover] and what the cover is for. Never what it pays or who it covers.

faq_slots.question: What happens if something isn't right after the job?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Open with what the customer does: tell us and we look at it. Then the reasonable care and skill standard every trade works to. No promise to come back free. Never invent a guarantee.

faq_slots.question: What happens when I ask for a quote in [TOWN]?
faq_slots.answer_brief: From [CV: quote_method] and the confirmed practices only: what the customer sends, what the business looks at (the surfaces and what they need before paint), what comes back. Where the town's conservation areas or listed homes bring a check in for an outside colour change, say it is settled before the work, with "usually"; whether the business handles it only from [CV: handles_planning]. No timescale unless [CV: response_time] is set.

faq_slots.question: When is the best time of year for [WORK_LOWER] work?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Inside, any time of year, with the reason the drying slows in a cold, damp room with no air moving. Outside, a dry, settled spell, and why from the paint's side: damp timber and masonry hold moisture under a new film, cold slows the drying, dew late in the day spoils the finish, and the limits are the chosen paint's own, not a season (the trade facts exterior rows). Where the town profile gives the exposure (a seafront, a hilltop, a damp valley), say what it does to that window. No temperature, no month, nothing about spring being busy or booking ahead, no promise about the weather.
